title: Resilience in Spring: Resilience4j, Spring Retry, timeouts and rate limits
seriesDescription: Kafka and RabbitMQ with Spring, retries, circuit breakers and timeouts. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Resilience4j circuit breaker, retry, rate limiter, bulkhead and time limiter in Spring Boot; Spring Retry and the Spring Framework 7 retry annotation; RestClient timeouts and proxy pitfalls.
source: Resilience4j documentation (Spring Boot 3 getting started, CircuitBreaker, Retry, RateLimiter, Bulkhead, TimeLimiter); Spring Retry README; Spring Framework reference (RestClient, resilience annotations); Spring Boot reference (HTTP client properties)

questions.prompt: Annotate getStock(String sku) so calls go through a Resilience4j circuit breaker named "inventory" and fall back to a method named stockFallback when the call fails or the circuit is open.
questions.model:
@CircuitBreaker(name = "inventory", fallbackMethod = "stockFallback")
public Stock getStock(String sku) { return client.fetch(sku); }
questions.explanation: The fallback must be in the same class with the same parameters plus an optional exception argument, e.g. stockFallback(String sku, Throwable t). Calls must cross the Spring proxy, so self-invocation does not trigger the breaker.

questions.prompt: Write the application.yml for a Resilience4j circuit breaker instance named inventory with a sliding window of 10 calls, a 50 percent failure-rate threshold, and 30 seconds in the open state before half-open.
questions.model:
resilience4j:
  circuitbreaker:
    instances:
      inventory:
        slidingWindowSize: 10
        failureRateThreshold: 50
        waitDurationInOpenState: 30s
questions.explanation: Spring Boot relaxed binding accepts both camelCase and kebab-case keys. Add permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState and slowCallDurationThreshold to also trip on latency.

questions.prompt: Extend the Resilience4j circuit breaker instance inventory in application.yml so that only java.io.IOException counts as a failure and com.example.NotFoundException is ignored (counted as neither success nor failure).
questions.model:
resilience4j:
  circuitbreaker:
    instances:
      inventory:
        recordExceptions:
          - java.io.IOException
        ignoreExceptions:
          - com.example.NotFoundException
questions.explanation: A 404-style business exception is not a sign of an unhealthy dependency, so ignoring it keeps it from skewing the failure rate. Without recordExceptions every exception counts as a failure (except the ignored ones).

questions.prompt: Write the application.yml for a Resilience4j retry instance named inventory with at most 4 attempts, a first wait of 200 ms, and exponential back-off with multiplier 2.
questions.model:
resilience4j:
  retry:
    instances:
      inventory:
        maxAttempts: 4
        waitDuration: 200ms
        enableExponentialBackoff: true
        exponentialBackoffMultiplier: 2
questions.explanation: maxAttempts includes the first call. Add enableRandomizedWait (with randomizedWaitFactor) for jitter and retryExceptions to restrict what is retried. Use @Retry(name = "inventory") on the method.

questions.prompt: Write the application.yml for a Resilience4j rate limiter instance named search that allows 10 calls per 1 second period and does not wait for a permit (rejects immediately).
questions.model:
resilience4j:
  ratelimiter:
    instances:
      search:
        limitForPeriod: 10
        limitRefreshPeriod: 1s
        timeoutDuration: 0
questions.explanation: With timeoutDuration 0 a call that finds no permit fails at once with RequestNotPermitted, which you would map to HTTP 429. A positive timeout makes callers wait for a permit instead.

questions.prompt: Match each Resilience4j module with the problem it addresses.

right.text: Stops calling a dependency that is failing or slow, then probes for recovery
Repeats a failed call a bounded number of times with a wait
Limits how many calls are permitted in a period
Limits concurrent calls so one dependency cannot take every thread
Bounds the duration of an asynchronous call

questions.explanation: Decorators compose. With the Spring Boot aspects the default order is Retry outside CircuitBreaker outside RateLimiter outside TimeLimiter outside Bulkhead.

questions.prompt: With the default Resilience4j Spring Boot aspect ordering, which decorator is the outermost one wrapping the others?

options.why: Bulkhead is the innermost decorator by default.
Correct: Retry wraps CircuitBreaker, RateLimiter, TimeLimiter and Bulkhead.
The breaker sits inside Retry, so each attempt is judged separately.
TimeLimiter sits inside the rate limiter and breaker, near the bottom.

questions.explanation: Retry outside the breaker means each retry attempt is seen (and may be rejected) by the breaker. You can change the order with the aspect-order properties.

questions.prompt: A Resilience4j breaker has slidingWindowSize = 10, minimumNumberOfCalls = 5 and failureRateThreshold = 50. The first calls all fail. After how many recorded calls can the breaker first open?
questions.explanation: Below minimumNumberOfCalls the failure rate is not evaluated, so the breaker stays CLOSED for calls 1 to 4. On the 5th recorded call the rate is 5 of 5 = 100 percent, which is at least 50, so it opens.

questions.prompt: A Resilience4j breaker is HALF_OPEN with permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState = 4 and failureRateThreshold = 50. After the 4 trial calls, what is the largest number of failed trials for which the breaker still returns to CLOSED?
questions.explanation: The breaker opens when the failure rate is greater than or equal to the threshold. 1 of 4 is 25 percent (closes), 2 of 4 is 50 percent (reopens), so at most 1.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: A Resilience4j @CircuitBreaker annotation has no effect when the annotated method is called with this.getStock(sku) from another method of the same class.
questions.reason: Spring applies the annotation through a proxy, and a call on this bypasses the proxy.

whys.a: Correct: The aspect only runs when the call goes through the proxy object, which a self-call does not.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Not this one: A is true while R is false does not describe this pair; check the truth of R again.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: Move the annotated method to another bean, inject the bean, or use the programmatic CircuitBreaker API (circuitBreaker.executeSupplier).

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: A fallbackMethod declared on @CircuitBreaker is also invoked when the circuit is open and the call is rejected.
questions.reason: The fallback only runs for exceptions thrown by the business method itself, never for exceptions raised by the breaker.

whys.a: Not this one: Both A and R are true and R explains A does not describe this pair; R does not explain A.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Correct: A is true: a rejected call raises CallNotPermittedException and the fallback can handle it. R is false.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: Declare a fallback overload for CallNotPermittedException if you want to treat a rejection differently from a real failure, for example by serving stale data.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: A Resilience4j @TimeLimiter can enforce a timeout on a plain synchronous method that returns String.
questions.reason: The TimeLimiter works by cancelling a Future or other asynchronous result when time runs out.

whys.a: Not this one: Both A and R are true and R explains A does not describe this pair; R does not explain A.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Not this one: A is true while R is false does not describe this pair; check the truth of R again.
whys.d: Correct: A is false: with the annotation the method must return a CompletableFuture or a reactive type. R is true and is the reason.

questions.explanation: For blocking code put a timeout on the HTTP client itself, or run the call in an executor and return its CompletableFuture.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: An ignoreExceptions entry in a Resilience4j breaker counts the ignored exception as neither a success nor a failure.
questions.reason: Spring Boot relaxed binding accepts both camelCase and kebab-case property keys.

whys.a: Not this one: Both A and R are true and R explains A does not describe this pair; R does not explain A.
whys.b: Correct: Both are true, but key spelling has nothing to do with how ignored exceptions are counted.
whys.c: Not this one: A is true while R is false does not describe this pair; check the truth of R again.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: Ignored exceptions are rethrown to the caller but do not touch the failure rate, which keeps business errors from tripping the circuit.

questions.prompt: Create a RestClient whose underlying SimpleClientHttpRequestFactory has a connect timeout of 2 seconds and a read timeout of 5 seconds.

checks.label: builds the client with the factory

questions.explanation: The JDK and most HTTP libraries default to no read timeout. With WebClient use .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5)) on the Mono plus Reactor Netty responseTimeout and CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MILLIS options. Boot 3.4+ also has spring.http.client.connect-timeout and read-timeout properties.

questions.prompt: Annotate a method fetchStock with Spring Retry so it runs at most 4 attempts in total on IOException, starting with a 200 ms delay that doubles each time.
questions.model:
@Retryable(retryFor = IOException.class, maxAttempts = 4, backoff = @Backoff(delay = 200, multiplier = 2))
public Stock fetchStock(String sku) throws IOException { ... }
questions.explanation: In Spring Retry, maxAttempts counts the original call (default 3). Needs @EnableRetry and a call through the Spring proxy (self-invocation bypasses it). Older versions spelled retryFor as include or value. Resilience4j @Retry(name = "x") is an equally valid answer in a Resilience4j project.

questions.prompt: Spring Framework 7's built-in @Retryable (org.springframework.resilience.annotation) is configured with maxRetries = 4. In the worst case, how many times is the method invoked in total?
questions.explanation: maxRetries counts retries after the initial call, so 1 + 4 = 5 invocations. Spring Retry's maxAttempts = 4 would have meant 4 invocations in total, a classic off-by-one when migrating.

questions.prompt: True or false: a Resilience4j circuit breaker can open because calls are too slow even when none of them throws an exception.

options.why: Correct: slowCallRateThreshold and slowCallDurationThreshold count slow calls toward opening.
The breaker is not only exception-driven; slow calls are counted separately.

questions.explanation: Configure slowCallDurationThreshold (for example 2s) and slowCallRateThreshold (for example 80). A call still must complete (or be cut off by a timeout) to be measured.

questions.prompt: Which signature is a valid fallback for @CircuitBreaker(name = "inventory", fallbackMethod = "stockFallback") on Stock getStock(String sku)?

options.text: Stock stockFallback(String sku, Throwable t) in the same class.
options.why: Correct: same parameters plus an optional exception, same return type.

options.text: void stockFallback() in any other class.
options.why: The fallback must return the same type and live in the same class.

options.text: Stock stockFallback(int sku) in the same class.
options.why: Parameter types must match the original method.

options.text: String stockFallback(String sku, Throwable t) in the same class.
options.why: The return type must be compatible with Stock, not String.

questions.explanation: Resilience4j picks the most specific matching fallback by exception type, so you can have one overload per exception class.
